response.report:
EXAM: Chest radiograph, one view, 2026-11-21
CLINICAL INDICATION: Emergency department. Shortness of breath. History of prostate cancer on hormone therapy. Portable film.
ORDERING PROVIDER: Dr. J. Marte, ED
COMPARISON: Chest radiograph, 2026-06-30
TECHNIQUE: Current is AP (labeled supine, portable) with low lung volumes. Prior is PA (appears upright). Projection, position and inspiration differ from the prior, so comparison is limited.

LOOK AT FIRST:
- F1 and F2: Increased hazy and reticular opacity in the right and left perihilar and mid zones (bilateral pattern).
- F9: Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen. These are indeterminate; the two blind reads disagreed (one read indeterminate, one read new). They could be an endotracheal tube and an enteric tube or central line, or external tubing.
- F3: Right basal opacity, indeterminate (both reads indeterminate).
- F7: Enlarged cardiac silhouette, indeterminate for change. Not time-sensitive, but listed in look-first order.

FINDINGS (systematic read, done blind to the indication):
- Airway / lungs: Trachea is roughly midline allowing for rotation. Lung volumes are low. There is diffuse bilateral hazy and reticular opacity, most marked in the perihilar and mid zones, with denser opacity at both bases. On the prior, the lungs were better inflated and largely clear, with mildly prominent perihilar and right lower zone markings. The right mid zone (F1) and left mid zone (F2) opacity is increased from the prior, and may reflect interstitial or alveolar fluid. Other diffuse processes are not excluded. Supine position and lower volumes contribute to some of the difference. Right basal opacity (F3) partly obscures the right hemidiaphragm and is indeterminate and not comparable. Retrocardiac and left basal opacity (F4) obscures the left hemidiaphragm and is indeterminate and not comparable. Low volumes and the magnified heart shadow may account for part of the basal opacity. No pleural line is seen, but the film is supine and sensitivity for pneumothorax is limited. No discrete lung mass is seen on this film, but the diffuse opacity and the left upper chest device generator hide lung.
- Mediastinum / hila: The upper mediastinum looks wide on an AP supine film with mild rotation. The prior PA showed no widening. Both hila are indistinct with surrounding hazy opacity. Width and hilar size cannot be reliably compared across projections.
- Pleura: Both costophrenic angles are hazy and both hemidiaphragms are partly obscured. A layering pleural effusion is possible on each side and is indeterminate (F5 right, F6 left). Only one of the two reads recorded each. The right costophrenic angle was clear on the upright prior. The left was not sharply defined on either study. Fluid amount is not comparable between supine and upright films.
- Heart: The cardiac silhouette is enlarged on both studies (F7). It looks larger on the current film, but the current film is AP supine with low volumes, which magnifies the heart. Size change is indeterminate and no change is reported. Heart borders are partly blurred by adjacent lung opacity.
- Bones / soft tissue: No displaced rib fracture or destructive bone lesion is seen at this resolution. No soft tissue gas. A mottled, heterogeneous density projects over the right glenoid and scapular neck region on the current film (F10). It could be a projectional effect from arm position and the overlying ECG electrode, or altered bone texture. It is indeterminate and not comparable with the prior. It needs review on the source images in PACS. Devices: a left chest wall cardiac device generator with transvenous leads is present, with a coil over the right mediastinum, a coiled lead over the lower heart and electrode markers over the left heart (F8). The configuration is broadly similar to the prior allowing for projection, and no lead discontinuity is seen at this resolution. External monitoring leads are present.

INTERVAL CHANGE:
- Changed: Bilateral perihilar and mid zone hazy and reticular opacity is increased (F1, F2). Linear densities that could be tubes or lines are not on the prior (F9). They are indeterminate because the reads disagreed. No size change is reported for the heart, the mediastinum or any opacity.
- Unchanged: Left chest wall cardiac device and lead configuration are stable allowing for projection (F8). Basal opacities (F3, F4), possible effusions (F5, F6), cardiac silhouette (F7) and the right scapular density (F10) are not comparable and cannot be called changed or unchanged.

RECIST 1.1: not computed on radiographs

CAN'T DETERMINE:
- Has the heart size changed? | Reason: Prior is PA and current is AP supine with low volumes. AP projection and low inspiration magnify the heart shadow. | Recommend: Repeat PA and lateral when the patient is able. Echocardiography if clinically relevant.
- Is the upper mediastinum widened? | Reason: The current film is AP supine with mild rotation, which widens the mediastinal shadow. Device leads cross the region. | Recommend: Repeat upright PA film when the patient is able, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Are pleural effusions present, and have they changed? | Reason: The current film is supine, so fluid layers posteriorly and shows only as haze. The prior is upright. The amounts are not comparable. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film, bedside ultrasound, or CT chest.
- Do the basal opacities reflect consolidation, collapse, layering fluid or low volumes? | Reason: Low inspiration and supine position crowd the lower zones and mimic basal opacity. The magnified heart hides the left base. | Recommend: Repeat film with good inspiration when the patient is able, or CT chest.
- Is there a pneumothorax? | Reason: No pleural line is seen, but on a supine film air collects anteriorly and at the bases and may not show. A skin fold or linen line and external wires cross the chest. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Are an endotracheal tube, enteric tube or central line present, and where are the tips? | Reason: Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen overlap device leads, external wires and the spine. The image is low resolution. | Recommend: Review the source image in PACS with edge enhancement and correlate with the bedside record of lines and tubes. Confirm tip positions before use.
- Are there small lung nodules, or lesions behind the heart or generator? | Reason: Diffuse opacity on the current film, the device generator over the left upper chest and the enlarged heart all hide lung. The AP portable film is lower quality than the PA prior. | Recommend: CT chest if clinically relevant, or repeat PA and lateral after the diffuse opacity clears.
- Is there free gas under the diaphragm? | Reason: The current film is supine. Free gas does not collect under the diaphragm in this position. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film if there is clinical concern.
- Is there a pleural effusion on either side, and has it changed? | Reason: The current film is supine, so fluid layers posteriorly and shows only as hazy density. Both costophrenic angles are indistinct on the current film and were clear on the upright PA prior. | Recommend: Upright or semi-erect film or decubitus views when the patient is able, or bedside ultrasound or CT chest.
- Is the upper mediastinum truly widened? | Reason: Supine AP projection with mild rotation widens the mediastinal shadow. The prior PA showed no widening. | Recommend: Repeat upright PA film when the patient is able, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Is the right basal opacity consolidation, atelectasis or layering fluid? | Reason: Low lung volumes and supine position crowd the base and obscure the hemidiaphragm. A frontal film alone cannot separate these. | Recommend: Repeat film with better inspiration, upright if possible, or CT chest.
- Where exactly is the endotracheal tube tip relative to the carina, and is there an enteric tube with its tip in the stomach? | Reason: The image is low resolution and the carina is not clearly defined. A tubular density over the upper abdomen could be an enteric tube or external tubing. | Recommend: Review the source image in PACS with windowing. Repeat the film if the tube positions remain unclear.
- Are there small nodules or subtle bone lesions on either study? | Reason: The device generator overlies the left upper and mid zones on both films. Diffuse opacity and portable technique on the current film hide fine detail. | Recommend: CT chest if clinically indicated. Review source images in PACS.

IMPRESSION:
1. Increased bilateral hazy and reticular perihilar and mid zone opacity (F1, F2) compared with the prior. This may reflect interstitial or alveolar fluid, and other diffuse processes are not excluded. Supine position and lower volumes contribute to some of the difference.
2. Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen (F9) are indeterminate. The two blind reads disagreed. They could be an endotracheal tube and an enteric tube or central line, or external tubing. Presence and tip positions cannot be confirmed on this image.
3. Right basal opacity (F3) is indeterminate and not comparable. It could be consolidation, atelectasis, layering fluid or an effect of low volumes. Left retrocardiac and basal opacity (F4) is likewise indeterminate.
4. Enlarged cardiac silhouette (F7). Change is indeterminate because the prior is PA and the current is AP supine.
5. Possible bilateral pleural effusions (F5, F6) are indeterminate. Pneumothorax and free gas cannot be excluded on this supine film.
6. Mottled density over the right scapula and glenoid region (F10) is indeterminate and needs source image review given the history of prostate cancer.
7. Left chest wall cardiac device and leads are stable allowing for projection (F8).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Review source images in PACS now, with windowing and edge enhancement, for tube and line positions, lead integrity and the right scapular density. Correlate with the bedside record of lines and tubes and confirm tip positions before use.
- Repeat PA and lateral chest radiograph, upright if possible with good inspiration, when the patient is able.
- Upright or decubitus film, or bedside ultrasound, for pleural effusion and pneumothorax assessment when the patient is able.
- CT chest if there is clinical concern, or if the opacities, mediastinal width or possible bone abnormality remain unresolved.
- Echocardiography if clinically relevant for the enlarged cardiac silhouette.

AI DRAFT: requires resident review and attending signature.
